text: You already know SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets from earlier in this path, but that vocabulary doesn't transfer to inference automatically — it has to be redefined. A generic ninety-nine-point-nine percent success SLO lifted from a typical web service misses most of what matters here, because an inference request can be successful by HTTP status code and still miss its real target by being too slow, or by arriving during a period the service can't actually sustain.

That's why inference needs three separate SLOs instead of one combined number. Latency, measured at p99, is the slowest one percent of requests — not the average, which hides exactly the tail that real users feel. Throughput is the sustained rate the service can serve while still meeting its latency target, not its theoretical maximum. Availability is the fraction of requests that get a correct, timely response at all. Each one can be violated while the other two look perfectly healthy.

Each SLI needs a precise definition, not a vague goal. Latency might be the percent of requests under three hundred milliseconds, measured at the load balancer over a rolling window. Availability might be the percent of non-error, non-timeout responses. Throughput deserves special attention: it should be defined conditionally on latency, because a sustained rate achieved only by making every request slower isn't a throughput win — it's trading the latency SLO away to hit a bigger number.

GPU-backed serving has failure modes a generic SLO framework misses entirely. A replica that hasn't finished loading model weights into VRAM can take minutes to become ready, so a latency SLO measured only in steady state will miss a very real spike during scaling events. And a shallow process health check can report healthy even after an out-of-memory crash or a failed model load, because it never actually exercises the model to confirm it's still serving correctly.

Measure latency, throughput, and availability separately, define each SLI precisely enough to alert on, and account for cold starts and GPU-specific failures that a generic health check would miss. That's what turns 'inference seems fine' into something you can actually verify. Next lesson applies this same discipline to disaster recovery — because model checkpoints and training infrastructure need backup and failover planning just as rigorous as any other critical system.
